summary.text: The Keeling Curve is a graph of carbon dioxide in Earth's air, built from continuous readings at Hawaii's Mauna Loa Observatory from 1958 to today.
Its steady climb gave the first significant evidence that CO₂ levels were rising rapidly, a rise caused by burning fossil fuels.
A yearly wiggle of about 6 ppm tracks Northern Hemisphere plants drawing CO₂ out of the air in spring and summer, then releasing it as they decay.

items.prompt: Each year the CO₂ reading at Mauna Loa peaks around May and falls until September. What mostly drives that drop?

options.label: The volcano releases less gas in summer
Northern plants growing and taking up CO₂
Warm oceans pulling extra gas out of the air
People burning less fuel in warm months

items.explain: Most land vegetation is in the Northern Hemisphere, and its spring and summer growth removes CO₂ through photosynthesis until the September low.

items.prompt: You want CO₂ readings that reflect the wider atmosphere rather than one patch of countryside. Which kind of site best fits that goal?

options.label: A dense forest where plants trade lots of gas
The edge of a big city full of traffic
A spot far from continents with bare ground
A sheltered valley where the air sits still

items.explain: Mauna Loa was picked because it is remote, far from continents, and has little vegetation to skew the readings.

items.prompt: In 1938 Guy Callendar compared old CO₂ readings and concluded that human emissions were raising them. Why did most scientists not accept this?

options.label: His readings were scattered and irregular
Everyone already knew CO₂ was falling
He blamed volcanoes instead of people
His numbers showed no change over time

items.explain: Callendar's conclusion was widely rejected because the measurements behind it were patchy.

items.prompt: Testing his instruments in forests, Keeling found more CO₂ at night than in the afternoon. What explains the night-time excess?

options.label: Cool night air dissolves extra gas from dew
Traffic and heating peak after dark
The sensors drift when there is no light
Plants and soils keep respiring at night

items.explain: Respiration by plants and soils adds CO₂ at night, while afternoon values better reflect the wider air.

items.prompt: Over the decades the curve has kept climbing, and the climb has sped up recently. What is causing the long-term rise?

options.label: Gas leaking from Mauna Loa's own vents
More plants decaying every autumn
The burning of fossil fuels
A slow natural rise in sunlight

items.explain: The rise in atmospheric CO₂ comes from fossil fuel combustion and has been accelerating in recent years.

items.prompt: Mauna Loa readings started in March 1958. By November 2018, roughly how much had average CO₂ climbed?

options.label: About 10 ppm
About 300 ppm
About 1,000 ppm
About 90 ppm

items.explain: The average rose from 313 ppm to 406 ppm, a climb of about 93 ppm.

paragraphs.heading: What the curve shows
paragraphs.text: The Keeling Curve is a graph that tracks carbon dioxide in Earth's air, both its build-up over the years and its swing within each year. It comes from nonstop readings at Hawaii's Mauna Loa Observatory, running from 1958 to the present. It carries the name of Charles David Keeling, the scientist who started the monitoring program and ran it until he died in 2005.

paragraphs.heading: Why it mattered
paragraphs.text: Keeling's readings gave the first significant evidence that carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the atmosphere was climbing fast. Many scientists say the curve is what first drew the world's attention to today's rise in CO₂. Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard professor of the history of science, counts it among the most important scientific works of the 20th century.

paragraphs.heading: Before Keeling
paragraphs.text: Before the 1950s, people measured CO₂ only now and then, at scattered places. In 1938 the engineer and amateur meteorologist Guy Stewart Callendar compared air records from Kew, taken in 1898–1901, with records from the eastern United States taken in 1936–1938. The older set averaged 274 parts per million by volume (ppm) and the newer one 310 ppm, and he concluded that human emissions were pushing CO₂ up. Most scientists did not accept his result, because the measurements were so patchy.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing Mauna Loa
paragraphs.text: Keeling, who worked at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography, was the first to measure CO₂ often and regularly, in Antarctica and on Mauna Loa from March 1958. During the International Geophysical Year of 1957–1958, money from the Weather Bureau let him put infrared gas analyzers at remote sites, including the South Pole and Mauna Loa. Mauna Loa was picked because it lies far from any continent and has no vegetation. To keep fumes from the volcano's vents out, the team sampled the ocean breeze above the thermal inversion layer and normalized the data to remove local contamination. When funding was cut in the mid-1960s the South Pole work stopped, but Keeling kept Mauna Loa going, and it still runs today.

paragraphs.heading: A steady climb
paragraphs.text: At Mauna Loa, average CO₂ went from 313 ppm in March 1958 up to 406 ppm by November 2018, and it is currently growing by about 2.48 ppm per year. Burning fossil fuels causes this rise, and the rise has been speeding up in recent years. Because CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, the climb matters a great deal for global warming. Ancient air bubbles trapped in polar ice show that CO₂ stayed between 275 and 285 ppm through the Holocene epoch, from 9,000 BCE onward, before it began rising sharply at the start of the nineteenth century.

paragraphs.heading: The yearly wiggle
paragraphs.text: On top of the climb, the curve rises and falls by about 6 ppm every year. This wiggle follows land plants, and most of those grow in the Northern Hemisphere, which holds most of Earth's land. CO₂ peaks in May, then drops through the northern spring and summer as new growth pulls it out of the air by photosynthesis. After a low in September it climbs again through fall and winter, as plants and leaves die and rot and give the CO₂ back.

paragraphs.heading: Passing 400 ppm
paragraphs.text: On May 9, 2013, the daily average at Mauna Loa went above 400 ppm. Estimates for earlier geologic eras suggest CO₂ had not been that high since the mid-Pliocene, some 2 to 4 million years back. Today about 100 sites around the globe track CO₂, and many isolated sites confirm the same long-term trend, though none has a record as long as Mauna Loa's.
